qt: to the Commission Dolors Montserrat (PPE), Juan Ignacio Zoido Álvarez (PPE), Javier Zarzalejos (PPE) Subject:

Following the recent invasion by immigrants in Ceuta, further arrivals on the Spanish coast on fast boats used by criminal networks to illicitly carry people and drugs from North Africa show that migratory pressure and mafia activity continue. Sánchez’s government has been unable to provide an impactful response. Over summer 2026, landings have occurred on beaches in Murcia and Andalusia, even in busy areas and in the middle of the day. Mostly coming from the Algerian coast, the vessels are equipped with high-powered engines, reach the Spanish coast in a few hours, land and then go back, making them difficult to detect and intercept. Representatives of agents on the ground have reported weaknesses in the Spanish maritime surveillance systems. These situations raise obvious questions about the Spanish Government’s ability to properly protect an EU external border and deliver on its commitments under the European Pact on Migration and Asylum. In view of the above: 1.
What does the Commission make of Spain’s management and the resources it has deployed?
Does it believe that the Spanish Government should urgently ramp up its capacities?
How does the Commission intend to demand and support a response that works?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.10.2026) The Commission takes note of the concerns raised regarding arrivals and crime on the Spanish coast. Under Articles 77 to 80 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union1 and the Schengen Borders Code2, responsibility for day‑to‑day management and control of external borders lies with Member States, while the EU framework establishes common standards and provides mechanisms for operational and financial support. Member States are required to comply with these obligations under the relevant EU rules. In this context, periodic Schengen evaluations and European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) vulnerability assessments for Spain have not identified deficiencies indicating noncompliance. The Commission considers that any need to reinforce national capacities, including maritime surveillance assets, should be assessed in light of migratory pressure, cross‑border crime and the need to safeguard integrity and security of the Schengen area. The EU already supports Member States, including Spain, through Frontex joint operations and the European Border Surveillance System3 integrated framework, as well as through cooperation with EU Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation and EU Agency for Criminal Justice Cooperation to combat smuggling and trafficking networks. This support also includes the implementation of the EU Action Plan Against Drug Trafficking4 which contains a dedicated action to tackle the criminal use of go-fast vessels and dedicated EU funding. Cooperation with North African partners, including Algeria, also forms part of a broader EU external action to address illegal migration.
1 Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union of 13 December 2007 — consolidated version, OJ C 202,
